_meta.title: Day 25 — GPIO and physical I/O
_meta.commit_message: fix: move hardware blocks after objective in prompt
_meta.purpose: Eight ordinary GPIO and physical-I/O questions of the kind the operator hits when wiring a Pi or an ESP32: reading a button, debugging i2cdetect, driving a servo with PWM, choosing between I2C and SPI, reading UART in Python, protecting a GPIO line from motor spikes, MQTT between a Pi and an ESP32, and a brownout under motor load. None is about this machine. Every one is answerable from engineering knowledge the model already has.
design_notes: Day 24 measured the same boundary on web development and came in at 3/24. This is the harder version of that test, and the reason is the vocabulary: web-development questions share almost no words with the LIVE HARDWARE READINGS block, but GPIO questions share nearly all of them. I2C, SPI, UART, serial, /dev/tty, ESP32 and Raspberry Pi all appear in the prompt's own hardware and identity sections. If the hardware blocks are going to intrude anywhere, it is here.

That overlap makes this session diagnostic rather than merely another sample. A Day 24 failure could be explained as the model reaching for the only concrete material in the window. A Day 25 failure on gpio-2 (i2cdetect) cannot be explained that way and not also implicate the premise machinery, because the prompt carries a real I2C bus reading that the question does not ask about.

Fix E (4b3341e) moved the hardware blocks after the objective and the routing sections before it. Its own retest on Day 24's web-4 came back 0/2 — both reps still answered about the capture card, at 30 and 31 words. So this session is NOT run on the assumption that hardware intrusion is fixed; it is run to measure how much of it survives the reorder, and on which shapes.

The open hypothesis from Day 24's commit message is budget starvation: SHORT (40 words) is handed to short questions with long answers, and all three web-4 reps spent their 40 words on the capture card before reaching the question. Six of the eight rows here are short questions with procedural answers, so per-rep word counts are recorded and the ceiling is judged against the answers rather than assumed. Word ceilings are not themselves a grading criterion.

Refusal vocabulary is a hard fail wherever it appears ('I have no GPIO pins', 'no I2C sensor is attached', 'I cannot read serial'). Every row asks how a thing works or how to do a thing. None asks the bot to perform anything on live hardware, so an absent device is at most a closing note and never a reason to withhold the steps.

Attribution to a block is a hard fail on every row. There is no block that carries any of this, so 'The LIVE HARDWARE READINGS block lists ...' in front of general knowledge is a fabrication about provenance — the exact failure the enumerate branch's attribution rule was written to prevent, misfiring on material it was never meant to cover.

objectives.prompt: How do I read a button press on a Raspberry Pi using Python?
pass_criteria: names RPi.GPIO or gpiozero as the library
shows or names the read call (GPIO.input(pin), or gpiozero Button.is_pressed / when_pressed)
names pull-up or pull-down configuration
names debounce (bouncetime, or a software debounce)
NO refusal on the grounds that no button or no GPIO is attached
NO attribution of the answer to a prompt block

objectives.prompt: I have an I2C sensor connected to my RPi but `i2cdetect -y 1` shows nothing. What should I check?
pass_criteria: names wiring — SDA/SCL swapped or loose, and ground not shared
names pull-up resistors on SDA/SCL
names enabling I2C via raspi-config (or dtparam=i2c_arm=on)
names address conflicts or the wrong bus number
treats the sensor as the OPERATOR's, not as a claim about this machine
NO reference to this machine's own I2C bus readings

objectives.prompt: How do I generate a PWM signal on an ESP32 to control a servo?
pass_criteria: names the ledc peripheral or MicroPython machine.PWM
names 50 Hz as the servo frame rate
gives duty cycle or pulse width for the travel range (roughly 1 ms / 1.5 ms / 2 ms, or the equivalent duty values for 0 / 90 / 180 degrees)
NO refusal on the grounds that no ESP32 is attached
NO attribution of the answer to a prompt block

objectives.prompt: What's the difference between I2C and SPI, and when would you choose each?
pass_criteria: I2C: two wires (SDA/SCL), addressable, multiple devices per bus, slower
SPI: four wires (MOSI/MISO/SCLK/CS), faster, no addressing — chip select per device
gives a use case for each (I2C for many slow sensors; SPI for displays, SD cards, ADCs, high throughput)
answers as general engineering knowledge, not from any block
NO enumeration of this machine's own buses in place of the comparison

objectives.prompt: How do I read serial data from a sensor over UART in Python?
pass_criteria: names pyserial (serial.Serial)
names the baud rate as something that must match the device
names ser.readline() or ser.read()
names a timeout and handling the empty/partial read
NO refusal on the grounds that no serial device is attached to this machine
NO reference to this machine's own ttyUSB/ttyACM state

objectives.prompt: I'm getting voltage spikes on my GPIO line when a motor switches. How do I protect the Pi?
pass_criteria: names a flyback / freewheeling diode across the motor
names galvanic isolation — optocoupler, or a relay/driver board
names a separate power supply for the motor with a common ground
names decoupling or bulk capacitors
gives the protection as a procedure rather than declining because no motor is present

objectives.prompt: How do I communicate between a Raspberry Pi and an ESP32 using MQTT?
pass_criteria: names a broker — mosquitto — and says where it runs
names paho-mqtt on the Pi
names umqtt (umqtt.simple / umqtt.robust) on the ESP32
describes topic structure and the publish/subscribe split between the two devices
NO claim that this machine currently has an ESP32 attached
NO refusal on the grounds that no ESP32 is attached

objectives.prompt: My RPi is brownout-rebooting when a motor draws current. What's the fix?
pass_criteria: says not to power the motor from the Pi's 5V rail / GPIO
names a separate supply for the motor with grounds tied together
names bulk capacitance across the motor supply to absorb the inrush
may name an adequate PSU or the undervoltage indicator as secondary
treats the Pi as the OPERATOR's, not as a claim about this machine
